text:
A suspension bridge carries load by converting the downward weight of the deck into tension in cables, then passing that tension into towers and anchorages that deliver it to the ground.

The process begins at the deck, which supports traffic, its own weight, and occasional wind or snow. The deck is hung from vertical suspender cables, also called hangers, spaced at regular intervals along its length. Each hanger pulls upward on the deck at one point, so the deck behaves like a beam resting on many closely spaced elastic supports rather than on a few distant piers. This keeps the bending within the deck modest, which is why a suspension bridge can span distances that would be impossible for a simple girder.

The upper ends of the hangers attach to the main cables, the defining element of the bridge. These huge cables, made of thousands of parallel steel wires bundled together, drape in a smooth curve between the towers. Because a cable is flexible, it can only carry load in tension, and it naturally settles into a shape in which every part is pulled along its own length. When the hangers pull down on the cable, the cable responds by pulling back along its curve. Under a load spread evenly along the deck, that curve is close to a parabola. The sag of the cable matters a great deal: the shallower the curve, the greater the tension needed to support the same load, so designers balance cable height against the size of the cable and the towers.

At the towers, the main cables pass over saddles, which are smooth supports on top that let the cable slide slightly and turn direction without kinking or being damaged. Here the cable's pull has both a horizontal and a vertical part. On each side of a tower the cable tugs inward and downward. If the spans on both sides are balanced, the horizontal pulls largely cancel, leaving mostly a vertical force pressing down on the tower. The towers therefore act mainly as columns in compression, carrying the combined weight of the cables and the deck down through their legs into foundations. Those foundations are usually massive concrete structures sunk into bedrock or deep sediment, spreading the load over enough area that the ground can bear it.

Past the towers, the cables continue to the anchorages at each end of the bridge. These are the part that resists the horizontal pull, which the towers cannot absorb on their own. At the outer ends, the cable splays into individual strands fixed to huge blocks of concrete or tunneled into solid rock. The anchorage works by sheer mass and by gripping the earth, holding the cable against being drawn inward. Without it, the cables would simply straighten and the whole bridge would collapse toward the center.

The complete path of load is therefore clear: from deck to hangers in tension, from hangers to main cables in tension, from cables to towers in compression, and from towers to foundations and into the ground, while the remaining horizontal pull travels along the cables into the anchorages. Stiffening trusses or aerodynamic box girders in the deck add resistance to twisting and fluttering in wind, but the central idea remains the same: tension in the cables gathers the load, and compression in the towers and anchorage resistance deliver it safely to the earth.
